\section{Variance partitioning and the intrinsic-difficulty decomposition}
A dominance (LMG/Shapley) analysis confirms the distances carry almost nothing: together the four explain only
$\approx 3\%$ of the variance in detection, no single factor dominates, and every VIF is $\approx 1$
(Table~\ref{tab:variance}) --- so the null is not an artefact of collinearity masking a real effect.
\IfFileExists{tables/variance.tex}{\input{tables/variance}}{}
Because the one apparent effect (visual
distance, below) turned out to be an animal-size confound, we pivot the hypothesis from \emph{novelty} to
intrinsic \emph{difficulty}: we promote the label-free scene properties --- low-light/IR
(\texttt{achromatic\_fraction}), clutter, and the night/IR flag, each computed per location from the frames
with no SAM\,3 run and no target label --- from nuisance covariates to predictors of interest, and test them
at the same bar. Table~\ref{tab:difficulty} decomposes the outcome. Taken \emph{with} an animal-size covariate
each difficulty signal \emph{appears} to validate (leave-species-out and leave-location-out
$\Delta\mathrm{MAE}\approx+0.017$, both significant), but a nested decomposition shows the gain is entirely
the size covariate: $\log$-area \emph{alone} carries it ($\Delta\mathrm{MAE}=+0.017$, $p=0.001/0.014$), while
low-light \emph{alone} does \emph{not} validate ($p=0.12/0.23$) and adds only $\approx+0.002$ over size. The
low-light effect is also far weaker than it first looks: the location-level night/IR--\texttt{pDetA}
correlation of $r=-0.377$ is an aggregation artefact (the ecological-correlation fallacy) --- at the cell level
it is only $-0.13$, and clutter's cell-level correlation is $0.00$. The intrinsic-difficulty pivot is
therefore \textbf{also null}: the only label-free property that predicts detection is animal size.
\IfFileExists{tables/difficulty.tex}{\input{tables/difficulty}}{}

\section{Out-of-sample validation}
% TODO: predictive-line figures.
Table~\ref{tab:cv} reports whole-group hold-out error against a mean-predictor baseline. This is the headline
result and it is a \textbf{null}: on both the location and the species schemes, and for both targets, no
distance model beats simply predicting the mean --- every $\Delta\mathrm{MAE}$ is within noise of zero and no
gain is significant under the paired group-bootstrap. \textbf{This is not an underpowered test.} The same GLM
and grouped cross-validation, on the same cells, \emph{do} detect a real signal when one exists: animal size
($\log$-area) validates out of sample at the identical bar ($\Delta\mathrm{MAE}=+0.017$, $p<0.017$ on both
schemes; Table~\ref{tab:difficulty}). A test that fires for size yet stays flat for the distances is evidence
of a genuine \emph{absence} of before-running label-free signal, not of low power.
\IfFileExists{tables/cv_validation.tex}{\input{tables/cv_validation}}{}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.52\textwidth]{figures/res_pred_vs_actual.pdf}
\caption[Out-of-sample predicted vs actual]{Out-of-sample predictions vs the truth for detection
(\texttt{pDetA}), on held-out species and locations. The predictions collapse onto the mean baseline (orange)
instead of tracking the diagonal (dashed) --- the distances carry no out-of-sample predictive power.}
\label{fig:predvsactual}
\end{figure}

\section{Species hold-out (H1): novelty and the size confound}
The primary novelty test --- leave-one-species-out over the pooled train+test species (99 species,
1025 scored cells) --- is in Tables~\ref{tab:gate1_species}--\ref{tab:cv_species}. Out-of-sample
prediction is not significant on any hold-out (Table~\ref{tab:cv_species}). The only coefficient whose CI
excludes zero, \emph{visual distance} (Table~\ref{tab:coefficients_species}), is positive --- meaning
more-novel species are detected \emph{better}, the reverse of what H1 predicts --- and is a \textbf{confound}:
visually-distinctive species are larger
(visual~$\leftrightarrow$~$\log$-area $r=0.22$) and larger animals score higher
($\log$-area~$\leftrightarrow$~pDetA $r=0.30$, the strongest raw correlate of the score). Adding an animal-size
covariate shrinks the visual coefficient from $+0.37$ to $+0.22$ (CI now spanning zero) while size itself
is the significant driver, so ``visual novelty helps'' was really ``bigger animals are easier''. Taxonomic
novelty is flat ($r\approx0.00$). Novelty does not predict transfer.
\IfFileExists{tables/gate1_measurement_species.tex}{\input{tables/gate1_measurement_species}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/coefficients_species.tex}{\input{tables/coefficients_species}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/cv_validation_species.tex}{\input{tables/cv_validation_species}}{}

\caption[The size confound]{The one label-free property that predicts detection: animal size. Per-cell

\section{False positives / hallucination}
The detection score conditions on the animal being present, so it measures recall, not hallucination. The
$1486$ \emph{hard negatives} (queries for absent species) ask the complementary question, and are the
closest the study comes to a validated before-running signal. SAM\,3 returns a masklet anyway about
$\mathbf{9.8\%}$ of the time. This hallucination rate does \emph{not} rise with taxonomic novelty
($r\approx+0.06$, n.s.); it \emph{falls} with visual distinctiveness ($r\approx-0.33$), and this survives an
animal-size control (partial $-0.37$) --- a genuine, size-independent, label-free correlate, though its
direction (``distinctive $=$ safer'') is the \emph{opposite} of ``novelty hurts''. Crucially it is a
\textbf{correlate, not a predictor}: predicting a held-out species' hallucination rate from visual distance
beats a mean baseline by only $+0.008$~MAE and \emph{just misses} out-of-sample significance ($p=0.053$;
Table~\ref{tab:fp}). Even the study's best signal does not clear the bar.
\IfFileExists{tables/false_positives.tex}{\input{tables/false_positives}}{}

\section{Ablations and robustness}
\paragraph{Factor ablation.} Refitting detection with each distance dropped in turn barely moves the fit or
the (null) out-of-sample gain (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}): no single distance carries signal. The only design
that changes anything is adding the animal-size covariate, which alone lifts the out-of-sample gain to
significance ($\Delta\mathrm{MAE}\approx+0.02$, $p\!\le\!0.02$) --- again consistent with size being the sole
real correlate. Removing the support covariate does not rescue a distance effect either. The variance
partition (Table~\ref{tab:variance}) tells the same story from the other direction.
\IfFileExists{tables/ablations.tex}{\input{tables/ablations}}{}

\paragraph{Design robustness.} The null is not an artefact of the encoder, the crop, the prompt, or the
distance functional (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}). Re-running the full leave-species-out and leave-location-out
procedure with a CLIP rather than DINOv2 encoder, a whole-frame rather than mask-cropped embedding, and a
distributional Fr\'echet or MMD rather than nearest-prototype distance each leaves the out-of-sample gain
indistinguishable from the baseline (all $\Delta\mathrm{MAE}\le0.007$, $p\ge0.10$, every 95\% CI spanning
zero). A generic ``animal'' prompt is included for completeness: prompting non-specifically collapses
per-species detection to a near-constant, mostly-zero target (mean \texttt{pDetA}$\approx0.14$, $73\%$ of cells
exactly zero),\footnote{A minority of clips were additionally skipped for GPU memory on the $16$\,GB card used
for this pass; they are scored as misses and add noise but do not drive the collapse, which is intrinsic to the
non-specific prompt.} so the distance model cannot beat --- and, fitting a degenerate target, underperforms ---
a mean predictor. Across every variant the label-free distances fail identically, confirming the null is a
property of the transfer problem, not of one modelling choice.
\IfFileExists{tables/robustness.tex}{\input{tables/robustness}}{}

\section{Independent replication (MammAlps)}
\label{sec:mammalps}
Every result so far reuses one frozen inference pass on one dataset, so the species and location experiments
are near-orthogonal overlays rather than statistically independent replications. To test the null on genuinely
independent data we re-ran the whole pipeline on \textbf{MammAlps}~\cite{mammalps} --- an Alpine camera-trap
tracker with a different continent, species pool, and (uniquely) real per-camera environment metadata. MammAlps ships box-only
ground truth, so an offline adapter emits each box as a filled-rectangle mask and the scorer reads bbox-HOTA
(\texttt{eval.prefer\_bbox}); mask-IoU against filled rectangles is near-zero (dataset mask mAP\,$\approx0.002$),
so box-IoU is the honest metric. The run yields $20$ cells over $5$ species (red deer, roe deer, hare, wolf,
and a single-cell fox) and $9$ cameras. Zero-shot SAM\,3 is non-degenerate here (pHOTA\,$\approx0.44$,
Table~\ref{tab:gate1_mammalps}); as on SA-FARI, association tracks detection almost exactly
($\mathrm{corr}(\texttt{pDetA},\texttt{pAssA})=0.999$, $13/20$ cells identical), so the replication is a
detection story.

\paragraph{The distance null holds, but as a consistency check --- not confirmation.} The pre-registered
label-free distance model (taxonomic\,+\,visual\,+\,environment) does not predict detection transfer
out-of-sample under either hold-out (leave-camera-out $\Delta\mathrm{MAE}=+0.067$, $95\%$~CI
$[-0.043,+0.144]$, $p=0.099$; leave-species-out $+0.014$, $p=0.410$; both intervals span zero,
Table~\ref{tab:replication_mammalps}), directionally consistent with the SA-FARI null. We read this as a
consistency check rather than independent confirmation, because at $n=20$ the out-of-sample test is
demonstrably underpowered: a \emph{genuinely} predictive per-cell feature --- SAM\,3's own mean confidence,
in-sample $r=+0.57$ ($p=0.009$) --- itself fails to validate ($\Delta\mathrm{MAE}=-0.03/-0.05$, $p>0.9$). A real
signal that cannot clear the bar shows the instrument, not the hypothesis, is the limiting factor here.
\IfFileExists{tables/gate1_measurement_mammalps.tex}{\input{tables/gate1_measurement_mammalps}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/replication_mammalps.tex}{\input{tables/replication_mammalps}}{}

\paragraph{The one feature that ``validates'' is a confound, not a finding.} Visual distance alone beats the
mean baseline on both schemes ($\Delta\mathrm{MAE}=+0.078/+0.080$, $p\approx0.01$), but this is spurious and is
reported only to be dismissed. Its association with detection is \emph{positive}
($r=+0.636$, $p=0.003$) --- the opposite direction to the novelty$\rightarrow$failure hypothesis
(more-novel animals are detected \emph{better}, not worse), driven by the two
large, high-footage deer species SAM\,3 detects best; it is confounded with support ($r=+0.60$ with
$n_\text{frames}$); and because visual distance is species-constant with tied values (red\,=\,roe\,=\,$0.40$,
hare\,=\,wolf\,=\,$0.15$), its leave-species-out ``validity'' reduces to a twin species standing in for the
held-out one --- exactly the species-constant-feature artefact the double cross-validation is designed to
reject. Removing the two rare, low-support species that anchor it (hare, wolf; $4/20$ cells) reverses the
correlation to $r=-0.33$ (n.s.) and erases the gain on both schemes. This is the same visual/size confound diagnosed on
SA-FARI, and it does not support H1.

\paragraph{Scope.} MammAlps exercises only three of the four distances (temporal and the familiarity proxy are
degenerate over the six-week window; taxonomic distance is near-constant across five species), scores a
different target regime (box-HOTA at $3$\,fps), and is underpowered by construction (a single-cell fox fold).
It therefore reinforces --- and does not contradict --- the SA-FARI null, but cannot serve as independent
confirmation of any positive result. A larger, mask-native second dataset remains the route to that.

\section{Independent replication (BURST)}
\label{sec:burst}
The larger, mask-native dataset MammAlps pointed to is BURST~\cite{burst}. Its animal subset --- the animal
LVIS classes of the validation split, streamed mask-native and prompted by class name --- yields $132$ video\,$\times$\,class
cells across $41$ species, an order of magnitude more leave-species-out groups than MammAlps, in a distinct
regime (internet/driving/movie video, not camera traps). Zero-shot SAM\,3 is again non-degenerate
(pHOTA\,$0.635$, Table~\ref{tab:gate1_burst}), and here the association target is genuine
($\mathrm{corr}(\texttt{pDetA},\texttt{pAssA})=0.76$; of the $71$ multi-object cells, none has \texttt{pAssA}
exactly equal to \texttt{pDetA}), so both components are testable.

\paragraph{A third convergent null.} Under leakage-free leave-species-out cross-validation the before-running
distances again fail to predict detection transfer: the combined distance model improves out-of-sample MAE by
only $+0.002$ ($p=0.374$), with visual ($+0.003$, $p=0.257$), taxonomic (full-taxonomy subset $-0.006$,
$p=0.952$) and environment ($-0.001$, $p=0.747$) all individually null, and the association specs null likewise
(Table~\ref{tab:replication_burst}). The result is robust to dropping the $19$ single-cell species and to a
size control. The lone near-signal, visual distance, is the familiar artefact: its correlation with detection
is $+0.17$ --- in the \emph{opposite} direction to the novelty hypothesis (more-novel animals detected better),
and a size confound (partial correlation given $\log$-area $+0.08$, $p=0.35$). Three datasets --- SA-FARI, MammAlps and BURST --- now converge on the same
before-running distance null.
\IfFileExists{tables/gate1_measurement_burst.tex}{\input{tables/gate1_measurement_burst}}{}
\IfFileExists{tables/replication_burst.tex}{\input{tables/replication_burst}}{}

\paragraph{Powered, but not proof.} On the same cells the after-running confidence controls do fire
(\texttt{conf\_mean\_score} $+0.035$, $p=0.004$; \texttt{conf\_atc} $+0.029$, $p=0.012$), a real contrast with
MammAlps, where nothing validated: at $132$ cells the pipeline is demonstrably alive, not a dead or
misconfigured test. This does not, however, license calling the distance null fully powered. The confidence win
runs mostly through a \emph{within}-species channel --- collapsing \texttt{conf\_mean\_score} to species means,
as a species-constant distance effectively is, drops its gain to $+0.004$ ($p=0.21$) --- whereas a distance can
only act \emph{between} species, where the correlations are at most $+0.37$ (visual, and in the
opposite direction to novelty) against confidence's $+0.50$. The design thus detects a large between-species predictor but is underpowered for a small
one. We therefore read BURST as a third convergent null --- no moderate-or-large before-running distance signal,
in a better-powered mask-native regime --- rather than positive proof, with the only validated predictor across
all three datasets remaining SAM\,3's own after-running detection confidence, a mechanistically near-circular,
non-novel signal.

\section{Cross-dataset synthesis}
\label{sec:cross_dataset}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_dataset} collects every feature tested, its numerical out-of-sample result, and the
dataset it was measured on. The pattern is consistent across all three: no before-running label-free distance
--- taxonomic, visual, or environment, alone or combined --- predicts detection or association transfer out of
sample; every gain over a mean predictor is within bootstrap noise of zero. The only near-signal, visual
distance, appears in the \emph{opposite} direction to the novelty hypothesis (more-novel animals detected
better, not worse) and dissolves under an animal-size control wherever it is examined. The single feature that validates is not a before-running distance at all but SAM\,3's own
\emph{after-running} detection confidence, and even that decisively only on the large SA-FARI sample; the same
animal-size confound is the only before-running quantity that ever reaches significance. The contribution is
this robust, thrice-replicated null, honestly bounded: consistent across a camera-trap and an
internet-video dataset, and powered enough on SA-FARI and BURST to exclude a moderate effect, but not a small
one.
